    Estimate the rate of spatial spread

    Source: R/classes-vctrs.R, R/inv-spread.R
    inv_spread_rate.Rd

    Estimates the radial rate of spread of an invasion from dated occurrence records with three established methods:

    Usage

    is_inv_spread(x)

inv_spread_rate(
  .data,
  time = NULL,
  lon = NULL,
  lat = NULL,
  origin = NULL,
  method = c("front", "first_record", "area"),
  quantile = 1,
  cell_size = 0.5,
  min_records = 1,
  conf_level = 0.95
)

    Arguments

    x

    An object to test.

    .data

    A data frame, inv_occurrence() table or sf POINT layer with dated records.

    time

    <tidy-select> Column with the record time (numeric year, Date or POSIXct). Defaults to the time column of an <inv_occurrence>.

    lon, lat

    <tidy-select> Coordinate columns.

    origin

    Numeric vector of length two giving the introduction point. Defaults to the mean location of the earliest records.

    method

    One of "front", "first_record" or "area".

    quantile

    Quantile of distances used as the range front with method = "front". Values below 1 reduce the effect of outlying records.

    cell_size

    Grid cell size for method = "first_record", in decimal degrees for geographic data or coordinate units for projected data.

    min_records

    Minimum cumulative number of records for a time step to be used.

    conf_level

    Confidence level for the rate interval in glance().

    Value

    An <inv_spread> tibble with columns time, distance_km (radius or cell distance) and n (records contributing). The fitted linear model is stored in the metadata; tidy() and glance() return the spread rate in km per time unit and autoplot() draws it.

    Details

    • "front": for each time step, the range radius is the quantile of distances from the origin of all records up to that time (the maximum when quantile = 1). The rate is the slope of radius on time.

    • "first_record": records are gridded into cells of cell_size; each cell is dated by its first record and its distance is that of its nearest first-year record. The rate is the slope of distance on first record time, the distance regression method (Gilbert et al. 2004).

    • "area": the cumulative occupied area is the convex hull of all records up to each time, converted to an equivalent radius sqrt(area / pi) (Skellam 1951). The rate is the slope of radius on time.

    References

    Gilbert, M., Gregoire, J.-C., Freise, J. F. and Heitland, W. (2004). Long-distance dispersal and human population density allow the prediction of invasive patterns in the horse chestnut leafminer Cameraria ohridella. Journal of Animal Ecology, 73, 459-468. doi:10.1111/j.0021-8790.2004.00820.x

    Skellam, J. G. (1951). Random dispersal in theoretical populations. Biometrika, 38, 196-218. doi:10.1093/biomet/38.1-2.196

    Examples

    occ <- inv_occurrence(cane_toad, lon = lon, lat = lat, time = year)
spread <- inv_spread_rate(occ, origin = c(145.79, -17.10), quantile = 0.95)
spread
#> # A <inv_spread>: 90 × 3
#> # Method:         front
#> # Origin:         145.79, -17.1
#> # Rate:           7.014 km per time
#>     time distance_km     n
#>    <dbl>       <dbl> <int>
#>  1  1935       0.616     1
#>  2  1936     172.       10
#>  3  1937    1113.       32
#>  4  1938    1125.       37
#>  5  1939    1122.       42
#>  6  1940    1124.       60
#>  7  1941    1124.       63
#>  8  1942    1124.       65
#>  9  1943    1130.       67
#> 10  1944    1140.       78
#> # ℹ 80 more rows
glance(spread)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 10
#>   method rate_km std.error conf.low conf.high r.squared  p.value     n origin_x
#>   <chr>    <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl> <int>    <dbl>
#> 1 front     7.01     0.669     5.68      8.34     0.555 3.64e-17    90     146.
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: origin_y <dbl>

inv_spread_rate(occ, origin = c(145.79, -17.10), method = "first_record")
#> # A <inv_spread>: 544 × 4
#> # Method:         first_record
#> # Origin:         145.79, -17.1
#> # Rate:           13.83 km per time
#>    cell     time distance_km     n

#>  2 291_-34  1936      21.0      70
#>  3 291_-36  1936      93.7      63
#>  4 291_-37  1936     125.       17
#>  5 292_-36  1936      54.6      28
#>  6 292_-38  1936     171.       34
#>  7 290_-33  1937      83.7      39
#>  8 290_-34  1937      44.6      70
